Sectors of the Indian Economy

An economy is best understood by studying its components. This chapter classifies economic activities in three different ways, shows how GDP and GVA are counted, explains underemployment and how to create more work, and asks why most workers still need protection.

Chapter Overview

What this chapter is about, at a glance

An economy is best understood when we study its components or sectors. Sectoral classification can be done on several criteria, and this chapter discusses three: primary, secondary and tertiary (by the nature of activity); organised and unorganised (by employment conditions); and public and private (by ownership of assets).

It begins with the three sectors and their interdependence, then shows how the value of goods and services is counted — only final goods and services, not intermediate ones — giving GDP, and more recently GVA. Using data for 1977–78 and 2017–18 it shows that while the tertiary sector has become the largest producer, employment has not shifted in the same way: the primary sector still employs the most people, producing only about one-sixth of GVA.

That gap produces underemployment, or disguised unemployment. The chapter discusses how to create more work — irrigation, transport and storage, cheap credit, industries in semi-rural areas, education and tourism — and the Right to Work (MGNREGA 2005, now the Viksit Bharat–G RAM G 2025).

Finally it contrasts the organised and unorganised sectors through the lives of Kanta and Kamal, and the public and private sectors, explaining why governments must spend on roads, electricity, health and education.

Primary sector

Activities that produce goods by exploiting natural resources — agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry; also called the agriculture and related sector.

Secondary sector

Natural products changed into other forms through manufacturing — spinning yarn, making sugar or gur, bricks from earth.

Tertiary sector

Activities that support production — transport, storage, communication, banking, trade — plus teachers, doctors, barbers; also called the service sector.

GDP

The value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year.

GVA

Gross Value Added — the contribution of the three sectors after adjusting for taxes and subsidies; India now reports sector shares in GVA.

Underemployment

People apparently working but all of them working less than their potential; also called disguised unemployment.

Organised vs unorganised

Organised: regular terms of employment, registered, benefits such as provident fund and paid leave. Unorganised: small scattered units outside government control, low-paid, insecure.

Right to Work

MGNREGA 2005 guaranteed 100 days of employment a year in rural areas in about 625 districts; in 2025 it was replaced by Viksit Bharat–G RAM G 2025.

  • Describe the historical shift between sectors in developed countries.
  • Explain why the tertiary sector has become the largest producer in India, and why employment has not shifted similarly.

  • Explain why workers in the unorganised sector need protection, and who they are.

Sectors of Economic Activities

People around us are engaged in various economic activities. Some produce goods, others produce services. One way of understanding them is to group them using an important criterion — these groups are called sectors.

The three sectors and what they do
SectorWhat it doesExamples
Primary (agriculture and related sector)Produces a good by exploiting natural resources; the product is a natural product. Forms the base for all other products.Cultivation of cotton, dairy, fishing, forestry, minerals and ores
Secondary (industrial sector)Changes natural products into other forms through manufacturing — in a factory, workshop or at home.Spinning yarn and weaving cloth from cotton fibre; sugar or gur from sugarcane; bricks from earth
Tertiary (service sector)Does not produce a good but aids or supports the production process; generates services.Transport, storage, communication, banking, trade; teachers, doctors, washermen, barbers, cobblers, lawyers, administrators, accountants; internet cafés, ATM booths, call centres, software companies

Why is the primary sector called primary? Because it forms the base for all other products that we subsequently make. Since most of the natural products we get are from agriculture, dairy, fishing and forestry, this sector is also called agriculture and related sector. The secondary sector gradually became associated with the different kinds of industries that came up, so it is also called the industrial sector; and because tertiary activities generate services rather than goods, it is also called the service sector.

The sectors are interdependent

Economic activities, though grouped into three categories, are highly interdependent:

  • If farmers refuse to sell sugarcane to a particular sugar mill, the mill will have to shut down — the secondary sector depends on the primary.
  • If companies decide not to buy cotton from the Indian market and import all they need, Indian cotton cultivation becomes less profitable, farmers may go bankrupt, and cotton prices will fall.
  • Farmers buy tractors, pumpsets, electricity, pesticides and fertilisers. If the price of fertilisers or pumpsets goes up, the cost of cultivation rises and profits fall.
  • People working in industry and services need food. If transporters strike and lorries refuse to carry vegetables and milk from rural areas, food becomes scarce in cities and farmers cannot sell their produce.
Let’s work these out

Classify the following occupations under primary, secondary and tertiary sectors: tailor, basket weaver, flower cultivator, milk vendor, fishermen, priest, courier, workers in match factory, moneylender, gardener, potter, bee-keeper, astronaut, call centre employee.

Teacher explanation

Suggested classification: Primary — flower cultivator, fishermen, gardener, bee-keeper. Secondary — tailor, basket weaver, workers in match factory, potter. Tertiary — milk vendor, priest, courier, moneylender, astronaut, call centre employee.

Comparing the Three Sectors — Counting GDP and GVA

How do we count the various goods and services and know the total production in each sector? With thousands of goods and services, we cannot add up cars, computers, nails and furniture. Economists therefore suggest that the values of goods and services should be used rather than the actual numbers. If 10,000 kg of wheat is sold at Rs 20 per kg, its value is Rs 2,00,000; the value of 5,000 coconuts at Rs 15 each is Rs 75,000.

There is one precaution. Not every good or service produced and sold needs to be counted — only final goods and services. Take a farmer who sells wheat to a flour mill for Rs 20 per kg. The mill grinds it and sells the flour to a biscuit company for Rs 25 per kg. The company uses the flour, sugar and oil to make four packets of biscuits and sells them for Rs 80 (Rs 20 per packet). Biscuits are the final goods — goods that reach the consumers.

Wheat and flour here are intermediate goods, used up in producing final goods. The value of final goods already includes the value of all intermediate goods used in making them: the Rs 80 for biscuits already includes the Rs 25 for flour and the Rs 20 for wheat. To count wheat and flour separately would be counting the same thing several times.

Definition

GDP: the value of final goods and services produced in each sector during a particular year gives the total production of that sector; the sum of production in the different sectors gives the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of a country — the value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year. GDP shows how big the economy is.

In India the mammoth task of measuring GDP is undertaken by a central government ministry, which — with the help of government departments of all states and union territories — collects information on the total volume of goods and services and their prices and estimates the GDP.

Recently the Indian government began to bring out the contribution of the three sectors towards Gross Value Added (GVA) in place of their contribution towards GDP, to be at par with global practices. GVA measures the contribution of the three sectors after adjusting for taxes and subsidies. (The difference between GDP and GVA is studied in higher classes; here we only see how production in the three sectors has changed.)

Historical Change in Sectors

From the histories of many now-developed countries, at initial stages of development the primary sector was the most important sector of economic activity. As methods of farming changed and agriculture prospered, it produced much more food than before; many people could take up other activities, and the number of craft-persons and traders increased. Buying and selling increased many times, and there were transporters, administrators and armies. But at this stage most goods were natural products and most people were employed in the primary sector.

Over a long time — more than a hundred years — and especially because new methods of manufacturing were introduced, factories came up and expanded. People who had worked on farms began to work in factories in large numbers, and began to use many more goods produced in factories at cheap rates. The secondary sector gradually became the most important in total production and employment. Hence, over time, a shift had taken place.

In the past 100 years there has been a further shift from secondary to tertiary sector in developed countries. The service sector has become the most important in terms of total production, and most working people are also employed in it. This is the general pattern observed in developed countries.

Most goods were natural products and most people worked in agriculture.
New manufacturing methods, factories expanded; people moved from farms to factories.
Services became the most important in production, and most workers moved into services — the pattern in developed countries.
Tertiary production became the largest, but employment remained in the primary sector.
Primary, Secondary and Tertiary Sectors in India

Graph 1 shows the production of goods and services in the three sectors for two years, 1977–78 and 2017–18 — chosen because the data are comparable and authentic. Total production has grown over the forty years.

Over these forty years, while production in all three sectors increased, it increased the most in the tertiary sector. As a result, in 2017–18 the tertiary sector emerged as the largest producing sector in India, replacing the primary sector.

Why is the tertiary sector becoming so important?

  1. Basic services: in any country, services such as hospitals, educational institutions, post and telegraph, police stations, courts, village administrative offices, municipal corporations, defence, transport, banks and insurance are required. In a developing country the government has to take responsibility for providing these.
  2. Development of agriculture and industry leads to the development of services such as transport, trade and storage — the more the primary and secondary sectors develop, the greater the demand for such services.
  3. Rising income levels: as incomes rise, certain sections demand many more services — eating out, tourism, shopping, private hospitals, private schools, professional training — seen most sharply in big cities.
  4. New services based on information and communication technology have become important and essential, and their production has been rising rapidly.

However, not all of the service sector is growing equally well. At one end there are a limited number of services employing highly skilled and educated workers; at the other end a very large number of workers are engaged as small shopkeepers, repair persons and transport persons who barely manage to earn a living, performing these services because no alternative opportunities exist. Hence only a part of this sector is growing in importance.

Where Are Most People Employed? Underemployment

A remarkable fact about India is that while there has been a change in the share of the three sectors in GVA, a similar shift has not taken place in employment. The primary sector continues to be the largest employer even now. Why? Because not enough jobs were created in the secondary and tertiary sectors.

Growth of production and employment, 1977–78 to 2017–18
SectorRise in productionRise in employment
Secondary (industry)More than 9 timesAround 3 times
Tertiary (services)14 timesAround 5 times

As a result, more than half of the workers in the country are working in the primary sector, mainly in agriculture, producing only about one-sixth of the GVA. The secondary and tertiary sectors produce the rest while employing less than half the people. Does this mean workers in agriculture are not producing as much as they could? What it means is that there are more people in agriculture than is necessary — even if a few people move out, production will not be affected. In other words, workers in the agricultural sector are underemployed.

Laxmi’s story

Laxmi’s case: a small farmer owning about two hectares of unirrigated land, dependent only on rain, growing crops like jowar and arhar. All five members of her family work on the plot throughout the year because they have nowhere else to go. Everyone is working, none remains idle, but their labour effort gets divided: each one is doing some work but no one is fully employed. This is underemployment — people are apparently working but all of them are made to work less than their potential. This kind of underemployment is hidden, in contrast to someone who has no job and is clearly visible as unemployed; hence it is also called disguised unemployment.

If a landlord, Sukhram, hires one or two members of the family to work on his land, the family earns extra wages, and since five people are not needed on that small plot, production is unaffected. Two people may even move to work in a factory; the family’s earnings would increase and they would continue to produce as much from their land. There are lakhs of farmers like Laxmi in India: even if we remove a lot of people from agriculture and provide them proper work elsewhere, agricultural production will not suffer, and the incomes of those who take up other work would increase the total family income.

This underemployment can happen in other sectors too. Thousands of casual workers in the service sector in urban areas search for daily employment as painters, plumbers and repair persons doing odd jobs; many do not find work every day. Others push a cart or sell something all day and earn very little — doing this work because they have no better opportunities.

How to Create More Employment

Take Laxmi with her two-hectare plot of unirrigated land. The government can spend money, or banks can give a loan, to construct a well so that she can irrigate and take a second crop, wheat, in the rabi season. Suppose one hectare of wheat provides employment to two people for 50 days (including sowing, watering, fertiliser application and harvesting) — then two more members of the family can be employed in her own field. If a new dam is constructed and canals are dug to irrigate many such farms, a lot of employment can be generated within agriculture itself, reducing underemployment.

If Laxmi and other farmers produce much more, they need to sell it. If the government invests in transportation and storage, or makes better rural roads so that mini-trucks reach everywhere, several farmers can continue to grow and sell crops — providing productive employment not just to farmers but also to those in transport and trade.

Laxmi also needs seeds, fertilisers, agricultural equipment and pumpsets. Being poor she cannot afford many of these, so she borrows from moneylenders at high interest. If a local bank gives her credit at a reasonable rate, she can buy these in time and cultivate her land. Along with water we also need cheap agricultural credit.

Another way is to identify, promote and locate industries and services in semi-rural areas where a large number of people may be employed. If many farmers grow arhar and chickpea, setting up a dal mill to procure and process them and sell in the cities is one example. Opening a cold storage lets farmers store potatoes and onions and sell when the price is good. In villages near forest areas, honey collection centres can be started. Industries that process vegetables and produce — potato, sweet potato, rice, wheat, tomato, fruits — can also be set up, providing employment in semi-rural areas rather than only in large urban centres.

In India about 60 per cent of the population belongs to the age group 5–29 years, and of these only about 51 per cent are attending educational institutions. The rest, particularly those under 18, may be at home or working as child labourers. If these children are to attend schools we will require more buildings, teachers and staff — a study by the erstwhile Planning Commission (now NITI Aayog) estimates that nearly 20 lakh jobs can be created in the education sector alone. Improving health requires many more doctors, nurses and health workers in rural areas. Every state or region has potential — tourism, regional craft industry, or new services like IT; the same study says that if tourism is improved, we can give additional employment to more than 35 lakh people every year.

Right to Work

Some suggestions take a long time to implement, so for the short term we need quick measures. Recognising this, the Union Government made a law implementing the Right to Work in about 625 districts of India. It was called the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005 (MGNREGA 2005): all those who are able to work and are in need of work in rural areas were guaranteed 100 days of employment in a year by the government, and if the government failed in its duty it would give unemployment allowances. The types of work that would help increase production from land were given preference. In 2025 this Act was replaced by the Viksit Bharat–Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Viksit Bharat–G RAM G 2025).

Do it yourself

What groups of people do you think are unemployed or underemployed in your area? Can you think of some measures that could be taken up for them?

Division of Sectors as Organised and Unorganised

Another way of classifying activities looks at the way people are employed: what are their conditions of work, and are there rules and regulations that are followed?

Kanta and Kamal — two working lives
Organised sector — KantaUnorganised sector — Kamal
Works in an office from 9.30 a.m. to 5.30 p.m.Daily wage labourer in a nearby grocery shop, 7:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.
Gets salary regularly at the end of every monthGets only his wages; not paid for days he does not work
Gets provident fund, medical and other allowancesNo other allowances, no leave or paid holidays
Does not work on Sundays — a paid holidayCan be asked to leave anytime by his employer
Given an appointment letter stating all terms and conditionsNo formal letter of employment

The organised sector covers enterprises or places of work where the terms of employment are regular and people therefore have assured work. They are registered by the government and have to follow its rules and regulations, given in laws such as the Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Gratuity Act and Shops and Establishments Act. It is called organised because it has some formal processes and procedures; some people may not be employed by anyone but work on their own, and even they have to register with the government and follow the rules.

Workers in the organised sector enjoy security of employment. They are expected to work only a fixed number of hours; if they work more they have to be paid overtime. They get paid leave, payment during holidays, provident fund, gratuity, medical benefits, and facilities such as drinking water and a safe working environment; when they retire they get pensions.

The unorganised sector is characterised by small and scattered units largely outside the control of the government. There are rules and regulations but they are not followed. Jobs are low-paid and often not regular; there is no provision for overtime, paid leave, holidays or sick leave. Employment is not secure — people can be asked to leave without reason, and when there is less work, as in some seasons, some may be asked to leave. A lot also depends on the whims of the employer. This sector includes a large number of people employed on their own doing small jobs such as selling on the street or repair work, and farmers who work on their own and hire labourers as and when required.

Table 2.3 — Workers in different sectors (in millions, late 1990s)
SectorOrganisedUnorganisedTotal

Total82394476
Total in percentageAbout 17%About 83%100%

Agriculture is an unorganised sector activity: it is not registered, employment is seasonal and there is no formal protection. Of the workers in the primary sector, 232 of 233 million are in the unorganised sector.

How to Protect Workers in the Unorganised Sector?

The organised sector offers jobs that are the most sought-after, but employment opportunities there have been expanding very slowly. It is also common to find many organised sector enterprises in the unorganised sector — they adopt such strategies to evade taxes and refuse to follow laws that protect labourers. As a result, a large number of workers are forced into unorganised sector jobs which pay a very low salary; they are often exploited and not paid a fair wage, their earnings are low and irregular, and the jobs are not secure and have no other benefits.

Since the 1990s it is also common to see a large number of workers losing their jobs in the organised sector, and these workers are forced to take up jobs in the unorganised sector with low earnings. Hence, besides the need for more work, there is also a need for protection and support of the workers in the unorganised sector.

Who are these vulnerable people? In rural areas the unorganised sector mostly comprises landless agricultural labourers, small and marginal farmers, sharecroppers and artisans (weavers, blacksmiths, carpenters and goldsmiths). Nearly 80 per cent of rural households in India are in the small and marginal farmer category; these farmers need support through adequate facility for timely delivery of seeds, agricultural inputs, credit, storage facilities and marketing outlets.

In urban areas the unorganised sector comprises mainly workers in small-scale industry, casual workers in construction, trade and transport, and those who work as street vendors, head-load workers, garment makers and rag pickers. Small-scale industry also needs government support for procuring raw material and marketing of output. Casual workers in both rural and urban areas need to be protected.

We also find that the majority of workers from scheduled castes, tribes and backward communities find themselves in the unorganised sector. Besides getting irregular and low-paid work, these workers also face social discrimination. Protection and support to unorganised sector workers is therefore necessary for both economic and social development.

Sectors in Terms of Ownership: Public and Private

Another way of classifying economic activities is on the basis of who owns assets and is responsible for the delivery of services. In the public sector the government owns most of the assets and provides all the services; in the private sector, ownership of assets and delivery of services is in the hands of private individuals or companies. Railways or the post office are examples of the public sector, whereas companies like Tata Iron and Steel Company Limited (TISCO) or Reliance Industries Limited (RIL) are privately owned.

Activities in the private sector are guided by the motive to earn profits, and to get such services we have to pay money to these individuals and companies. The purpose of the public sector is not just to earn profits; governments raise money through taxes and other ways to meet expenses on the services they render.

Why do governments spend on certain activities?

  1. Some things are needed by society as a whole but the private sector will not provide them at a reasonable cost — because they need spending large sums of money beyond the capacity of the private sector, and collecting money from thousands of users is not easy. Even if provided, they would be charged at a high rate. Examples: construction of roads, bridges, railways, harbours, generating electricity, irrigation through dams.
  2. Some activities need government support, because the private sector may not continue them otherwise. Selling electricity at the cost of generation may push up production costs in many industries and small units might have to shut down, so the government produces and supplies electricity at rates industries can afford and bears part of the cost. Similarly, the government buys wheat and rice from farmers at a “fair price”, stores it in godowns and sells at a lower price through ration shops, bearing part of the cost — supporting both farmers and consumers.
  3. Some activities are the primary responsibility of the government — providing health and education facilities for all. Running proper schools and providing quality education, particularly elementary education, is the duty of the government; India’s illiterate population is one of the largest in the world. Nearly half of India’s children are malnourished and a quarter of them are critically ill, and the infant mortality rate of Odisha (36) or Madhya Pradesh (43) is higher than some of the poorest regions of the world. Government must also attend to safe drinking water, housing for the poor, food and nutrition, and must take care of the poorest and most ignored regions through increased spending.
Teacher explanation

Why do governments spend on health and education, even though these are not profitable? — Because they are the primary responsibility of the state, they benefit society as a whole, and the private sector will not provide them adequately at a reasonable cost.

Flashcards

All key terms

Key terms and definitions
TermSimple explanation
SectorA group of economic activities classified using a particular criterion — nature of activity, employment conditions, or ownership.
Primary sectorActivities that produce goods by exploiting natural resources — agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry, minerals; also called the agriculture and related sector.
Secondary sectorActivities that change natural products into other forms through manufacturing — also called the industrial sector.
Tertiary sectorActivities that support production and generate services — transport, storage, communication, banking, trade, education, health; also called the service sector.
Intermediate goodsGoods used up in producing final goods — wheat and flour in the biscuit example.
Final goods and servicesGoods and services that reach the consumer; only these are counted while measuring total production.
GDPGross Domestic Product — the value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year.
GVAGross Value Added — the contribution of the three sectors after adjusting for taxes and subsidies; now used in place of GDP for sector shares.
UnderemploymentA situation where people are apparently working but all of them are made to work less than their potential.
Disguised unemploymentUnderemployment that is hidden — everyone appears employed, as on Laxmi’s two-hectare plot, though the labour is more than the land needs.
Organised sectorEnterprises where terms of employment are regular, registered by the government and covered by laws such as the Factories Act and Minimum Wages Act; workers get security and benefits.
Unorganised sectorSmall, scattered units largely outside government control; jobs are low-paid, irregular and insecure, with no provision for overtime or paid leave.
Right to WorkThe guarantee of employment under MGNREGA 2005 — 100 days a year in rural areas in about 625 districts; replaced in 2025 by Viksit Bharat–G RAM G 2025.
MGNREGA 2005Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005: 100 days of guaranteed employment a year for those able and in need of work in rural areas, with unemployment allowance if the state fails.
Viksit Bharat–G RAM G 2025Viksit Bharat–Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission, which replaced MGNREGA in 2025.
Public sectorActivities in which the government owns most of the assets and provides the services — railways, post office.
Private sectorActivities in which ownership of assets and delivery of services is with private individuals or companies — TISCO, Reliance Industries Limited.
Gross Value AddedSee GVA — value of output after adjusting for taxes and subsidies.
MalnutritionPoor nutrition; the chapter notes that nearly half of India’s children are malnourished and a quarter critically ill.
Small and marginal farmersFarmers with small holdings; nearly 80 per cent of rural households in India fall in this category and need support.

NCERT In-text Questions and Answers

The questions printed inside the chapter

These are the “Can you…” and activity questions that appear inside the chapter text. Model answers are based on the chapter itself.

1.

Complete the table to show how sectors are dependent on each other.

Model answer

Examples: sugarcane farmers → sugar mill (primary supplies secondary); cotton growers → textile mill; farmers → fertiliser and tractor makers (secondary supplies primary); factories and offices → transporters, shopkeepers, banks (tertiary serves both); mill workers → farmers for food (primary feeds secondary and tertiary).

2.

Explain the difference between primary, secondary and tertiary sectors using examples other than those mentioned in the text.

Model answer

Primary: fishing — catching fish from the sea, a natural product. Secondary: a bakery — flour and sugar are processed into bread and biscuits. Tertiary: a bus service — it produces no good but moves people and goods, supporting both other sectors.

3.

Classify the following occupations under primary, secondary and tertiary sectors: tailor, basket weaver, flower cultivator, milk vendor, fishermen, priest, courier, workers in match factory, moneylender, gardener, potter, bee-keeper, astronaut, call centre employee.

Model answer

Primary: flower cultivator, fishermen, gardener, bee-keeper. Secondary: tailor, basket weaver, workers in match factory, potter. Tertiary: milk vendor, priest, courier, moneylender, astronaut, call centre employee.

4.

Students in a school are often classified into primary and secondary or junior and senior. What is the criterion used? Do you think this is a useful classification? Discuss.

Model answer

The criterion is the level or stage of schooling. It is useful for organising teaching, syllabi and facilities appropriate to each stage — but, like all classifications, it tells us only what the criterion measures, and says nothing about a student’s ability or talent.

5.

What does the history of developed countries indicate about the shifts that have taken place between sectors?

Model answer

At early stages the primary sector was most important. With new manufacturing methods, factories expanded and the secondary sector became most important in production and employment. In the past 100 years there has been a further shift to the tertiary sector, which is now the most important in production, with most workers employed in services.

6.

Correct and arrange the important aspects for calculating GDP from this jumble: “To count goods and services we add the numbers that are produced. We count all those that were produced in the last five years. Since we shouldn’t leave out anything we add up all these goods and services.”

Model answer

Corrected: to count goods and services we add their values, not their numbers; we count only final goods and services, not intermediate ones; and we count only those produced within the country during a particular year (not the last five years).

7.

Discuss with your teacher how you could calculate the total value of a good or service using the method of value added at each stage.

Model answer

Take the biscuit example: wheat Rs 20, flour Rs 25, biscuits Rs 80. Value added at each stage is 20 (farmer), 5 (mill), 55 (biscuit company) — and 20 + 5 + 55 = 80, which equals the value of the final good. So adding value added at each stage gives the same answer as counting final goods once.

8.

Looking at Graph 1: which was the largest producing sector in 1977–78 and which in 2017–18? Which sector grew the most over forty years? What was the GDP of India in 2017–18?

Model answer

The primary sector was the largest producer in 1977–78; the tertiary sector was the largest in 2017–18. The tertiary sector grew the most. The chapter’s graph axis goes up to Rs 1,40,00,000 crore, but the exact GDP figure is not printed in the text — read it off the graph in your textbook.

9.

Look at the following examples. Which of these are unorganised sector activities? (i) A teacher taking classes in a school (ii) A headload worker carrying a bag of cement (iii) A farmer irrigating her field (iv) A doctor in a hospital treating a patient (v) A daily wage labourer working under a contractor (vi) A factory worker going to work in a big factory (vii) A handloom weaver working in her house.

Model answer

Unorganised: (ii) headload worker, (iii) farmer irrigating her field, (v) daily wage labourer under a contractor, (vii) handloom weaver working in her house. Organised: (i) teacher in a school, (iv) doctor in a hospital, (vi) factory worker in a big factory.

10.

Talk to someone who has a regular job in the organised sector and another who works in the unorganised sector, and compare their working conditions.

Model answer

Ask about: written appointment, fixed hours, overtime payment, paid leave and holidays, provident fund, gratuity, medical benefits, pension, job security and safety at work. Organised workers will report most of these; unorganised workers usually report none, and often no written contract at all. (Student activity.)

11.

Complete Table 2.3 and answer: what percentage of workers in the unorganised sector are in agriculture? Do you agree that agriculture is an unorganised sector activity? Why? What percentage of workers in India are in the unorganised sector, and what percentage in the organised sector?

Model answer

The table totals are: primary 233, secondary 115, tertiary 128, all sectors 476 million; organised 82 million, unorganised 394 million. Agriculture accounts for 232 of the 233 million primary-sector workers — about 59 per cent of all unorganised workers (232 of 394). Yes, agriculture is unorganised: it is not registered, employment is seasonal, there is no formal contract or protection. Overall about 83 per cent of workers are in the unorganised sector and only about 17 per cent in the organised sector.

12.

Why do you think MGNREGA 2005 or Viksit Bharat–G RAM G 2025 is referred to as “Right to work”?

Model answer

Because it gives a legal guarantee: everyone in rural areas who is able to work and needs work has a right to 100 days of employment a year, and if the government fails to provide it, it must pay an unemployment allowance. Work becomes an enforceable right rather than a favour.

13.

Imagine you are the village head. Suggest some activities under this Act that would also increase people’s income.

Model answer

Digging and repairing irrigation channels, farm ponds and wells; building all-weather village roads; land levelling and soil conservation; planting and protecting trees; constructing check dams for groundwater recharge; building cattle sheds and compost pits. Each creates durable assets that raise farm output and therefore incomes. (Student answers will vary.)

14.

How would income and employment increase if farmers were provided with irrigation and marketing facilities?

Model answer

Irrigation allows a second crop, so the same land employs more people for more days; assured water raises yields. Marketing facilities — storage, transport, mandis and fair prices — reduce distress sales and raise the farmer’s realization, and create work in transport, storage and trade. Higher incomes then raise demand for other goods and services.

15.

In what ways can employment be increased in urban areas?

Model answer

By supporting small-scale industry and services with credit, raw material and marketing; by building infrastructure — transport, water, sanitation — which itself creates work; by expanding education and health services; by promoting tourism and IT-enabled services; and by giving street vendors and casual workers secure spaces and conditions so that their work becomes more productive.

08

NCERT Exercise Questions and Answers

End-of-chapter exercises, projects and activities

NCERT Exercises

Reproduced from the exercise section of the chapter, with model answers. Word limits are the ones the textbook sets.

1.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Fill in the blanks: (i) Employment in the service sector ___ increased to the same extent as production. (ii) Workers in the ___ sector do not produce goods. (iii) Most of the workers in the ___ sector enjoy job security. (iv) A ___ proportion of labourers in India are working in the unorganised sector. (v) Cotton is a ___ product and cloth is a ___ product. (vi) The activities in primary, secondary and tertiary sectors are ___.

Model answer

(i) has not (ii) tertiary (iii) organised (iv) large (v) natural; manufactured (vi) interdependent.

2.
NCERT exercise4 marks

Choose the most appropriate answer. (a) Sectors are classified into public and private on the basis of: (i) employment conditions (ii) the nature of economic activity (iii) ownership of enterprises (iv) number of workers. (b) Production of a commodity mostly through the natural process is an activity in the ___ sector: (i) primary (ii) secondary (iii) tertiary (iv) information technology. (c) GDP is the total value of ___ produced during a particular year: (i) all goods and services (ii) all final goods and services (iii) all intermediate goods and services (iv) all intermediate and final goods and services. (d) In terms of GVA the share of the tertiary sector in 2017–18 is between ___ per cent: (i) 20 to 30 (ii) 30 to 40 (iii) 50 to 60 (iv) 60 to 70.

Model answer

(a) (iii) ownership of enterprises (b) (i) primary (c) (ii) all final goods and services (d) (iii) 50 to 60 per cent.

3.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Match the following — problems faced by the farming sector with some possible measures: (1) Unirrigated land (2) Low prices for crops (3) Debt burden (4) No job in the off season (5) Compelled to sell grains to local traders soon after harvest — with (a) setting up agro-based mills (b) cooperative marketing societies (c) procurement of food grains by government (d) construction of canals by the government (e) banks to provide credit with low interest.

Model answer

(1) → (d) construction of canals by the government; (2) → (c) procurement of food grains by government; (3) → (e) banks to provide credit with low interest; (4) → (a) setting up agro-based mills; (5) → (b) cooperative marketing societies.

4.
NCERT exercise4 marks

Find the odd one out and say why. (i) Tourist guide, dhobi, tailor, potter, farmer (ii) Teacher, doctor, vegetable vendor, lawyer (iii) Postman, cobbler, soldier, police constable (iv) MTNL, Indian Railways, Air India, All India Radio.

Model answer

(i) Farmer — the others are tertiary-sector services; farming is primary (the tailor and potter are secondary, so the odd one is the only primary activity). (ii) Vegetable vendor — the others are professional services requiring formal training; the vendor is a trader. (iii) Cobbler — the others are government (public sector) employees. (iv) All India Radio — it is a public broadcaster, while MTNL, Indian Railways and Air India are public sector enterprises providing transport or telecom services. (Answers can be argued; state your criterion.)

5.
NCERT exercise3 marks

A research scholar looked at working people in Surat: 15% organised in offices and factories registered with the government; 15% own shops, offices or clinics in marketplaces with formal licence; 20% working on the street, construction workers, domestic workers; the rest working in small workshops usually not registered. Complete the table. What is the percentage of workers in the unorganised sector in this city?

Model answer

The four groups are 15 + 15 + 20 + 50 = 100 per cent (the unregistered workshops account for 50 per cent). The organised sector is the first two groups — offices and factories registered with the government (15%) and own shops with formal licence (15%) = 30 per cent. The unorganised sector is the remaining 70 per cent (20% street, construction and domestic workers + 50% in unregistered workshops).

6.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Do you think the classification of economic activities into primary, secondary and tertiary is useful? Explain how.

Model answer

Yes. It lets us see where output comes from and where people work, and therefore reveals problems — in India the tertiary sector produces the most while the primary sector still employs the most, and more than half the workers produce only about one-sixth of GVA. That single comparison explains underemployment and points to the need for more jobs in industry and services.

7.
NCERT exercise3 marks

For each of the sectors why should one focus on employment and GVA? Could there be other issues which should be examined? Discuss.

Model answer

Employment tells us how many people depend on a sector for their living; GVA tells us how much that sector contributes to the economy. Reading them together shows productivity and underemployment. Other issues worth examining: working conditions and security, wages, the organised–unorganised divide, the environment, gender composition of the workforce, and regional inequality.

8.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Make a long list of all kinds of work that you find adults around you doing for a living. In what way can you classify them? Explain your choice.

Model answer

For example: farmer, dairyman, carpenter, tailor, mechanic, bus conductor, teacher, nurse, shopkeeper, software engineer, domestic worker, vegetable vendor. Classify by nature of activity (primary: farmer, dairyman; secondary: carpenter, tailor, mechanic; tertiary: the rest), and also by employment conditions (organised or unorganised) and by ownership (public or private). State which criterion you used and why. (Student answers will vary.)

9.
NCERT exercise3 marks

How is the tertiary sector different from other sectors? Illustrate with a few examples.

Model answer

It does not produce a good; it supports the production of goods by others. Transport moves what farmers and factories produce, storage keeps it, banking provides credit, trade sells it, and teachers, doctors and barbers provide services directly. Its output is a service, not a physical product.

10.
NCERT exercise3 marks

What do you understand by disguised unemployment? Explain with an example each from urban and rural areas.

Model answer

Disguised unemployment is underemployment that is hidden: everyone appears to be working, but the work could be done by fewer people. Rural: Laxmi’s family — five members work all year on a two-hectare unirrigated plot; two could leave without reducing output. Urban: a family of four running a small shop where two could manage, or several casual painters and plumbers sharing the few jobs available.

11.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Distinguish between open unemployment and disguised unemployment.

Model answer

Open unemployment: a person has no job at all and is clearly visible as unemployed. Disguised unemployment: people appear employed — everyone is working — but all are working below their potential, so some could leave without any fall in output.

12.
NCERT exercise5 marks

“Tertiary sector is not playing any significant role in the development of the Indian economy.” Do you agree? Give reasons.

Model answer

I disagree. The tertiary sector is now the largest producing sector in India, replacing the primary sector, and its production rose 14 times between 1977–78 and 2017–18. It provides basic services such as education, health, banking and transport on which the other sectors depend, and new IT-based services are growing rapidly. Its weakness is employment: service employment rose only about five times, and much of the sector consists of low-productivity work by small shopkeepers and casual labourers. So it is significant in production, but has not solved the employment problem.

13.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Service sector in India employs two different kinds of people. Who are these?

Model answer

At one end, a limited number of highly skilled and educated workers — professionals in IT, finance, medicine, education and administration, earning well. At the other end, a very large number of small shopkeepers, repair persons, transport persons and casual workers who barely manage to earn a living, doing this work because no alternative opportunities exist.

14.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Workers are exploited in the unorganised sector. Do you agree with this view? Give reasons.

Model answer

Yes. Jobs there are low-paid and irregular, there is no provision for overtime, paid leave, holidays or sick leave, employment is not secure and people can be asked to leave without reason; rules exist but are not followed, and much depends on the employer’s whims. Many organised enterprises also operate through the unorganised sector to evade taxes and labour laws, and since the 1990s workers losing organised jobs have been pushed into such work. Workers from scheduled castes, tribes and backward communities also face social discrimination there.

15.
NCERT exercise3 marks

How are the activities in the economy classified on the basis of employment conditions?

Model answer

Into organised and unorganised. The organised sector has regular terms of employment, is registered and follows laws such as the Factories Act and Minimum Wages Act, and gives security, fixed hours, overtime, paid leave, provident fund, gratuity and pension. The unorganised sector consists of small scattered units outside government control, where rules are not followed and jobs are low-paid and insecure.

16.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Compare the employment conditions prevailing in the organised and unorganised sectors.

Model answer

Use Kanta and Kamal: Kanta works fixed hours, is paid monthly, gets provident fund, medical allowances and paid Sundays, and has an appointment letter. Kamal works 7:30 a.m. to 8 p.m., is paid only for days worked, gets no allowances, leave or holidays, has no letter, and can be asked to leave anytime. In short: security and benefits versus insecurity and low pay.

17.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Explain the objective of implementing MGNREGA 2005 or Viksit Bharat–G RAM G 2025.

Model answer

To provide a legal guarantee of work in rural areas — 100 days of employment a year to those able and in need of work — with an unemployment allowance if the government fails, and with preference for work that increases production from land. It is a short-term measure to raise incomes and reduce distress while longer-term measures take effect.

18.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Using examples from your area, compare and contrast the activities and functions of private and public sectors.

Model answer

Public: a government school or hospital, the post office, the state bus service, the municipal water supply — provided at low or no direct cost, aiming at service rather than profit. Private: a coaching centre, a private clinic, a private bus operator, a shop — charging fees and aiming at profit. Both may exist side by side, but the public one serves those who cannot pay. (Student answers will vary.)

19.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Discuss and fill the table giving one example each from your area of a well-managed and a badly managed organisation in the public and private sectors.

Model answer

For example: well-managed public — the local government hospital or a municipal school with regular staff; badly managed public — a water supply office with irregular service; well-managed private — a bank branch or a factory with good safety records; badly managed private — a shop that sells expired goods. Judge by service quality, punctuality, safety and accountability. (Student answers will vary.)

20.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Give a few examples of public sector activities and explain why the government has taken them up.

Model answer

Railways, post office, roads, bridges, harbours, dams and irrigation, electricity generation and supply, government schools and hospitals, and the PDS. Reasons: they need spending beyond the capacity of the private sector and it is difficult to collect money from thousands of users; the private sector would charge high rates or not provide them at all; some activities need support to continue (electricity at affordable rates, fair prices for farmers); and health and education are the primary responsibility of the government.

21.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Explain how the public sector contributes to the economic development of a nation.

Model answer

It builds the infrastructure — roads, railways, ports, power, irrigation — on which all private activity depends; it supplies electricity and credit at affordable rates and buys crops at fair prices, supporting farmers and small industry; it provides health and education which build human capital; it develops backward regions and looks after the poorest; and it provides services in areas where profit-seeking firms would not go. Together these raise productivity and make growth possible.

22.
NCERT exercise5 marks

The workers in the unorganised sector need protection on the issues of wages, safety and health. Explain with examples.

Model answer

Wages: a head-load worker or garment maker is paid low and irregular wages with no overtime — minimum wages must be enforced. Safety: construction and factory workers face accidents, and street vendors and rag pickers work in unsafe conditions — safety standards and inspection are needed. Health: casual workers get no medical leave or insurance, so one illness pushes a family into debt — health cover, crèches and drinking water at workplaces are needed.

23.
NCERT exercise5 marks

A study in Ahmedabad found that out of 15,00,000 workers, 11,00,000 worked in the unorganised sector. The total income of the city in 1997–98 was Rs 60,000 million, of which Rs 32,000 million was generated in the organised sector. Present this data as a table. What kind of ways should be thought of for generating more employment in the city?

Model answer

Table: organised — 4,00,000 workers (about 27%) generating Rs 32,000 million (about 53% of income); unorganised — 11,00,000 workers (about 73%) generating Rs 28,000 million (about 47%). So nearly three-fourths of workers produce less than half the income — a clear productivity gap. Ways to generate employment: support small-scale industry and services with credit and marketing; improve infrastructure; expand education, health and tourism; give street vendors secure vending zones; and train workers so they can move into more productive jobs.

24.
NCERT exercise5 marks

The following table gives GVA in rupees (crore) by the three sectors: 2001–02 — primary 13,23,000; secondary 10,40,000; tertiary 19,31,000. 2021–22 — primary 24,79,400; secondary 40,73,000; tertiary 73,25,000. (i) Calculate the share of the three sectors for both years. (ii) Show the data as a bar diagram. (iii) What conclusions can we draw?

Model answer

(i) Total 2001–02 = 42,94,000 crore: primary 30.8%, secondary 24.2%, tertiary 45.0%. Total 2021–22 = 1,38,77,400 crore: primary 17.9%, secondary 29.4%, tertiary 52.8%. (ii) Draw three bars per year with these percentages. (iii) The tertiary sector’s share rose from 45% to about 53% and the secondary from 24% to 29%, while the primary sector’s share fell from about 31% to 18% — confirming that services have become the largest and fastest-growing part of the economy, though employment has not shifted at the same pace.

09

Important Questions and Answers

Board-style practice

Practice questions

Written in the style of CBSE board papers. They are additional practice, not NCERT originals.

1.

Explain the three sectors of economic activity with two examples each. (5 marks)

Model answer

Primary: goods are produced by exploiting natural resources and the product is natural — cultivation of cotton, dairy, fishing, forestry. Secondary: natural products are changed into other forms through manufacturing in a factory, workshop or at home — spinning yarn and weaving cloth, making sugar or gur from sugarcane, bricks from earth. Tertiary: activities that do not produce a good but support production — transport, storage, communication, banking, trade; also teachers, doctors, barbers, lawyers. The tertiary sector generates services, hence it is called the service sector.

2.

How are the three sectors interdependent? Give examples. (3 marks)

Model answer

If farmers refuse to sell sugarcane, the sugar mill shuts down. If companies import all their cotton, Indian cotton farmers lose profits and prices fall. If fertiliser or pumpset prices rise, farmers’ costs rise and profits fall. And if transporters strike, food becomes scarce in cities while farmers cannot sell their produce. Each sector depends on the other two.

3.

Why are only final goods and services counted while measuring GDP? (3 marks)

Model answer

Because the value of final goods already includes the value of all intermediate goods used to make them. In the biscuit example, the Rs 80 for biscuits includes the Rs 25 for flour, which includes the Rs 20 for wheat. Counting wheat, flour and biscuits separately would count the same value several times. Hence GDP is the value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year.

4.

What is GVA and why is it used? (2 marks)

Model answer

Gross Value Added measures the contribution of the three sectors after adjusting for taxes and subsidies. The Indian government now brings out sector contributions in GVA instead of GDP to be at par with global practices.

5.

Why has the tertiary sector become the largest producing sector in India? (5 marks)

Model answer

(i) Basic services — hospitals, schools, post and telegraph, police, courts, defence, transport, banks, insurance — are required by everyone, and in a developing country the government must provide them. (ii) The development of agriculture and industry increases demand for transport, trade and storage. (iii) As incomes rise, people demand more services — eating out, tourism, shopping, private hospitals and schools, professional training. (iv) New services based on information and communication technology have become important and are growing rapidly. But not all of the sector grows equally: many small shopkeepers and casual workers barely earn a living.

6.

Why has employment not shifted out of the primary sector even though production has? (3 marks)

Model answer

Because not enough jobs were created in the secondary and tertiary sectors. Industrial production rose more than nine times but industrial employment only about three times, and service production rose 14 times while service employment rose about five times. So more than half the workers remain in the primary sector, producing only about one-sixth of GVA.

7.

Explain underemployment and disguised unemployment with Laxmi’s example. (5 marks)

Model answer

Laxmi owns about two hectares of unirrigated land, dependent on rain, growing jowar and arhar. All five family members work on the plot all year because they have nowhere else to go. Everyone is working, none is idle, but the labour is divided so that no one is fully employed: this is underemployment — people apparently working but all made to work less than their potential. Because it is hidden — unlike open unemployment, where a person has no job at all — it is called disguised unemployment. If a landlord hires two members, or if two move to a factory, production on the plot is unaffected and family income rises.

8.

Suggest five measures to increase employment in rural India. (5 marks)

Model answer

(i) Irrigation — wells, canals and dams — so that a second crop is possible and more labour is needed. (ii) Investment in transport and storage, including rural roads, so produce can be sold. (iii) Cheap agricultural credit from banks instead of moneylenders, for seeds, fertiliser and equipment. (iv) Setting up industries and services in semi-rural areas — dal mills, cold storage, honey collection centres, fruit and vegetable processing. (v) Expanding education and health services, which need teachers and health workers — about 20 lakh jobs are possible in education alone; tourism can add over 35 lakh jobs a year. In the short term, the Right to Work guarantees 100 days of employment.

9.

Distinguish between the organised and unorganised sectors. (5 marks)

Model answer

Organised: terms of employment are regular, enterprises are registered and follow laws such as the Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Gratuity Act and Shops and Establishments Act; workers have assured work, fixed hours with overtime, paid leave and holidays, provident fund, gratuity, medical benefits, safe working conditions and pensions. Unorganised: small scattered units largely outside government control; rules exist but are not followed; jobs are low-paid and irregular, with no overtime, paid leave or sick leave; employment is insecure and people can be asked to leave without reason; it includes street sellers, repair workers and farmers hiring labour as needed.

10.

Why do workers in the unorganised sector need protection? Who are they? (5 marks)

Model answer

Because their earnings are low and irregular, jobs are insecure, there are no benefits, and they are often exploited and denied fair wages; many organised enterprises also operate through the unorganised sector to evade taxes and labour laws, and since the 1990s retrenched organised workers have been pushed into it. In rural areas they are landless agricultural labourers, small and marginal farmers (nearly 80 per cent of rural households), sharecroppers and artisans; in urban areas, workers in small-scale industry, casual construction, trade and transport workers, street vendors, head-load workers, garment makers and rag pickers. A majority of workers from scheduled castes, tribes and backward communities are also here and face social discrimination, so protection is needed for both economic and social development.

11.

Why does the government undertake certain activities instead of leaving them to the private sector? (5 marks)

Model answer

(i) Some things needed by society as a whole will not be provided by the private sector at a reasonable cost — roads, bridges, railways, harbours, electricity generation, irrigation — because they need very large spending beyond private capacity and it is difficult to collect money from thousands of users. (ii) Some activities need support to continue: electricity must be supplied at rates small industries can afford, and wheat and rice must be bought at a fair price and sold cheaply through ration shops, so the government bears part of the cost. (iii) Health and education are the primary responsibility of the government — running proper schools and providing quality education is a duty of the state, and India’s illiteracy, malnourishment and high infant mortality in states such as Odisha (36) and Madhya Pradesh (43) show why. (iv) Government must also provide safe drinking water, housing, food and nutrition and look after the poorest and most ignored regions.

10

Previous Year Questions (PYQs)

Asked in CBSE board exams

Previous year questions

These follow the pattern of questions set in CBSE Social Science papers for this chapter. Answers are model answers.

1.
CBSE pattern

Distinguish between the primary and tertiary sectors with examples. (CBSE pattern, 3 marks)

Model answer

The primary sector produces goods by exploiting natural resources and its product is natural — farming, fishing, dairy. The tertiary sector produces no good; it supports production by providing services — transport, storage, banking, trade, teaching, health care. Primary output is a thing; tertiary output is a service.

2.
CBSE pattern

What is GDP? Why is it counted only for final goods? (3 marks)

Model answer

GDP is the value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year. Only final goods are counted because their value already includes the value of all intermediate goods used in making them; counting intermediate goods too would double-count the same production.

3.
CBSE pattern

Why is the primary sector still the largest employer in India? (3 marks)

Model answer

Because not enough jobs were created in the secondary and tertiary sectors — industrial employment grew about three times against a nine-fold rise in output, and service employment about five times against a fourteen-fold rise in production. Workers therefore stay in agriculture, where they are underemployed.

4.
CBSE pattern

What is the difference between open and disguised unemployment? (2 marks)

Model answer

Open unemployment is when a person has no job at all and is visibly unemployed. Disguised unemployment is when people appear to be working but are working below their potential, so some could leave without any fall in output.

5.
CBSE pattern

How does the public sector contribute to development? Give two examples. (3 marks)

Model answer

It builds infrastructure — roads, railways, power, irrigation — that private producers use; it supplies electricity and credit at affordable rates and buys crops at fair prices; and it provides health and education which build human capital, as well as services in backward regions where firms would not go. Examples: Indian Railways, government schools and hospitals.

6.
CBSE pattern

State any three benefits enjoyed by organised sector workers. (3 marks)

Model answer

Security of employment with fixed working hours and overtime payment; paid leave, holidays, provident fund and gratuity; and medical benefits, safe working conditions and pension on retirement.

7.
CBSE pattern

Why is the service sector important for India? (3 marks)

Model answer

Because it is the largest producing sector, contributing the biggest share of GVA, providing basic services such as education, health, banking and transport, generating foreign exchange through IT services, and creating new jobs — though its employment growth has lagged behind its output growth.

8.
CBSE pattern

What is the Right to Work? (2 marks)

Model answer

The legal guarantee of employment under MGNREGA 2005 — 100 days of work a year in rural areas in about 625 districts, with an unemployment allowance if the government fails to provide work. In 2025 it was replaced by the Viksit Bharat–G RAM G 2025.

9.
CBSE pattern

Who are the vulnerable workers in the unorganised sector? (3 marks)

Model answer

In rural areas: landless agricultural labourers, small and marginal farmers, sharecroppers and artisans. In urban areas: workers in small-scale industry, casual workers in construction, trade and transport, street vendors, head-load workers, garment makers and rag pickers.

10.
CBSE pattern

How can more employment be created in semi-rural areas? (2 marks)

Model answer

By locating industries and services there — dal mills, cold storage, honey collection centres and units processing vegetables and fruit — so that people find work near their villages rather than migrating to cities.

11

Frequently Asked Questions

Quick clarifications

1.

Is a teacher in the primary sector because she works in a “primary” school?

Model answer

No. Teaching is a tertiary activity — it provides a service. “Primary sector” refers to activities that draw directly on natural resources.

2.

Why is the tertiary sector called the service sector?

Model answer

Because its activities generate services rather than goods — transport, banking, trade, teaching, health care.

3.

Does GDP include goods produced by foreigners in India?

Model answer

Yes — GDP counts what is produced within the country, whoever produces it. That is why it is called Gross Domestic Product.

4.

Why do we now hear about GVA instead of GDP?

Model answer

Because the government began reporting sector contributions in GVA to be at par with global practice; GVA adjusts for taxes and subsidies.

5.

Is a street vendor employed or unemployed?

Model answer

Employed, but in the unorganised sector, and often underemployed — working long hours for very little income because no better opportunity exists.

6.

Are all government employees in the public sector?

Model answer

Yes — the public sector is defined by government ownership of assets and responsibility for delivering the service.

7.

Why does the government run ration shops at a loss?

Model answer

Because it buys wheat and rice at a fair price from farmers, stores it, and sells it cheaper to consumers, bearing part of the cost — supporting both farmers and poor consumers.

8.

Which sector produces the most in India today?

Model answer

The tertiary sector, which became the largest producing sector by 2017–18, replacing the primary sector.

12

Assertion-Reason Questions

Choose the correct option

How to answer

(a) Both A and R are true and R explains A. (b) Both are true but R does not explain A. (c) A is true, R is false. (d) A is false, R is true.

1.

Assertion (A): The three sectors are interdependent.
Reason (R): If farmers refuse to sell sugarcane, the sugar mill will have to shut down.

2.

Assertion (A): Only final goods and services are counted while measuring GDP.
Reason (R): The value of final goods already includes the value of intermediate goods used in making them.

3.

Assertion (A): The tertiary sector is the largest employer in India.
Reason (R): The tertiary sector is the largest producer in India.

4.

Assertion (A): Workers in the primary sector are underemployed.
Reason (R): More than half the workers produce only about one-sixth of GVA.

5.

Assertion (A): MGNREGA guaranteed 100 days of employment a year.
Reason (R): It was enacted in 2005 and covered about 625 districts.

6.

Assertion (A): Organised sector workers enjoy security of employment.
Reason (R): The organised sector is registered and follows laws such as the Minimum Wages Act.

7.

Assertion (A): Agriculture is an unorganised sector activity.
Reason (R): 232 of the 233 million primary-sector workers are in the unorganised sector.

8.

Assertion (A): The private sector provides health and education for all.
Reason (R): Health and education are the primary responsibility of the government.

9.

Assertion (A): The government supplies electricity at rates small industries can afford.
Reason (R): Selling electricity at the cost of generation would raise production costs and could force small units to shut down.

10.

Assertion (A): Underemployment is also called disguised unemployment.
Reason (R): In such a situation people appear to be working but all are working below their potential.

Source-Based and Case-Based Questions

Read the passage or table, then answer

Source 1 — Kanta and Kamal

Case study

Kanta works in an office. She attends her office from 9.30 a.m. to 5.30 p.m. She gets her salary regularly at the end of every month. In addition to the salary, she also gets provident fund as per the rules laid down by the government. She also gets medical and other allowances. Kanta does not go to office on Sundays. This is a paid holiday. When she joined work, she was given an appointment letter stating all the terms and conditions of work.

Kamal is Kanta’s neighbour. He is a daily wage labourer in a nearby grocery shop. He goes to the shop at 7:30 in the morning and works till 8:00 p.m. in the evening. He gets no other allowances apart from his wages. He is not paid for the days he does not work. He has therefore no leave or paid holidays. Nor was he given any formal letter saying that he has been employed in the shop. He can be asked to leave anytime by his employer.

1.

List three benefits Kanta gets that Kamal does not.

Model answer

A regular monthly salary with provident fund and medical allowances; a paid Sunday holiday and paid leave; and an appointment letter setting out the terms of employment. Kamal has none of these.

2.

How many hours does Kamal work compared with Kanta?

Model answer

Kamal works from 7:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. — about 12.5 hours — against Kanta’s eight hours, yet with no overtime, leave or security.

3.

Which sector does each belong to, and what determines the difference?

Model answer

Kanta is in the organised sector, Kamal in the unorganised sector. The difference is that organised enterprises are registered, follow laws such as the Factories Act and Minimum Wages Act, and must give security and benefits; unorganised units are small, scattered and largely outside government control.

Source 2 — Laxmi’s two hectares

Case study

Take the case of a small farmer, Laxmi, owning about two hectares of unirrigated land dependent only on rain and growing crops like jowar and arhar. All five members of her family work in the plot throughout the year. Why? They have nowhere else to go for work. You will see that everyone is working, none remains idle, but in actual fact, their labour effort gets divided. Each one is doing some work but no one is fully employed.

1.

Why do all five members work on the plot?

Model answer

Because they have nowhere else to go for work — there are no alternative employment opportunities.

2.

Why is this called disguised unemployment rather than open unemployment?

Model answer

Because nobody appears unemployed — everyone is working — but the work is shared out so that all are working below their potential. The unemployment is hidden.

3.

What two things could raise this family’s income without reducing farm output?

Model answer

A well or canal for irrigation, allowing a second crop (wheat) and more days of work; and one or two members taking wage work elsewhere, since the plot does not need all five.

Source 3 — Table 2.3, workers by sector

1.

What share of all workers are in the unorganised sector?

Model answer

394 of 476 million — about 83 per cent. Only about 17 per cent are in the organised sector.

2.

Which sector has almost no organised employment?

Model answer

The primary sector — 1 million organised against 232 million unorganised, which is why agriculture is described as an unorganised sector activity.

3.

What does this table imply for policy?

Model answer

That protection and support for unorganised workers — in wages, safety, health, credit and marketing — is essential, because they are the overwhelming majority of the workforce.

1.

No map work is set in this chapter. Instead, sketch a bar diagram of the three sectors’ shares in GVA for 2001–02 and 2021–22 using the exercise data, and label the fastest-growing sector.

Model answer

2001–02: primary 30.8%, secondary 24.2%, tertiary 45.0%. 2021–22: primary 17.9%, secondary 29.4%, tertiary 52.8%. The tertiary sector is the fastest-growing and largest in both years.

2.

Draw a pie chart of employment in the organised and unorganised sectors (late 1990s) and write one conclusion.

Model answer

Organised about 17% (82 of 476 million), unorganised about 83% (394 million). Conclusion: the overwhelming majority of Indian workers are outside formal protection.

3.

Show on a simple chart the rise in production and employment, 1977–78 to 2017–18, for industry and services.

Model answer

Industry: production ×9, employment ×3. Services: production ×14, employment ×5. The gap between the two bars is the employment problem.

4.

On an outline map of India, mark one state you associate with each of these: a high share of services (e.g. Karnataka), a high share of industry, and a state where agriculture dominates employment.

Model answer

Answers will vary; for example Karnataka (IT services), Gujarat or Maharashtra (industry) and Bihar or Uttar Pradesh (agriculture-dominated employment). Use the map to discuss regional differences in sectoral composition.

HOTS and Competency-Based Questions

Think beyond the text

Higher order thinking

These ask you to apply, compare or evaluate. Model answers are indicative — your own well-reasoned answer can differ.

1.

A state’s GVA grows by 8 per cent a year but its employment grows by only 1 per cent. What problems will follow, and what should the state do?

Model answer

Growth without jobs means more output per worker but few new opportunities: underemployment persists in agriculture, young people migrate or remain unemployed, and inequality widens because the gains go to owners of capital and skilled workers. The state should push labour-intensive sectors — construction, tourism, food processing, small-scale manufacturing — invest in education and skills so workers can take new jobs, support small producers with credit and infrastructure, and use schemes such as the Right to Work as a short-term measure. (Model answer.)

2.

“Counting GDP without counting employment is like counting a school’s success only by its buildings.” Discuss.

Model answer

Both are partial measures. GDP tells us how much is produced but not how many people have work, what they are paid or whether the work is secure. India’s case shows this: the tertiary sector produces the most while the primary sector employs the most, and more than half the workers produce only about one-sixth of GVA. A school judged only by its buildings might have no teachers; an economy judged only by GDP might have growth with underemployment. Both need distribution and quality measures. (Model answer.)

3.

Why might a worker prefer a lower-paid organised job to a higher-paid unorganised one?

Model answer

Because the organised job brings security and benefits that the higher wage does not: fixed hours with overtime, paid leave, provident fund, gratuity, medical facilities, safety at work and a pension. An unorganised job can end any day, has no leave, and one illness can wipe out the extra earnings. In Kanta and Kamal’s case, Kanta’s package is worth more than the wage alone. (Model answer.)

4.

Suggest a plan for a district where 70 per cent of workers are in agriculture and yields are stagnant.

Model answer

(i) Water: wells, canals or watershed structures so a second crop is possible. (ii) Credit at reasonable rates from banks and cooperatives instead of moneylenders. (iii) Storage and roads so produce is not sold at harvest-time low prices. (iv) Agro-processing in semi-rural areas — dal mill, cold storage, fruit and vegetable units — to create non-farm work. (v) Skills and education so the young can take service jobs; and (vi) the Right to Work as a safety net while these take effect. (Model answer.)

5.

Why does the government supply electricity below cost to industry but charge households for it? Argue both ways briefly.

Model answer

The chapter’s logic: selling electricity at the cost of generation would push up production costs, and many small units might shut down, so the government bears part of the cost to keep industry viable and employment intact. The counter-argument: subsidies must be paid for by someone — taxpayers or other consumers — and may encourage wasteful use. A reasoned answer should state the employment and industrial argument and the fiscal and efficiency argument, then take a position. (Model answer.)

6.

If you were advising a village panchayat, which three employment measures from the chapter would you rank first, and why?

Model answer

Likely ranking: (i) irrigation — it raises output and labour demand on the same land and creates a second season; (ii) rural roads and storage — they let produce reach markets and create work in transport and trade; (iii) a semi-rural processing unit such as a dal mill or cold storage — it creates non-farm jobs locally and reduces distress sales. Each is locally feasible, builds a durable asset and raises incomes. (Model answer; rankings may differ if justified.)
