Quick Revision Sheet

One page before the exam

Three sectors

  • Primary = natural products (agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry).
  • Secondary = manufacturing (yarn, sugar, bricks).
  • Tertiary = services (transport, storage, banking, trade, teaching, health).
  • They are interdependent — sugar mill needs farmers; farmers need fertiliser and transport.

Counting output

  • Use values, not numbers.
  • Only final goods and services; intermediate goods already included.
  • GDP = value of all final goods and services produced within the country in a year.
  • GVA = contribution after adjusting for taxes and subsidies; now used for sector shares.

Historical shift

  • Primary → secondary → tertiary in developed countries.
  • India: tertiary became the largest producer by 2017–18, but employment stayed in the primary sector.

Employment gap

  • Industry: production ×9, employment ×3. Services: production ×14, employment ×5.
  • More than half the workers → about one-sixth of GVA.
  • Underemployment = disguised unemployment (Laxmi’s five workers on two hectares).

Creating work

  • Irrigation (1 ha wheat = 2 people × 50 days), transport and storage, cheap credit.
  • Semi-rural industries: dal mill, cold storage, honey centres, food processing.
  • Education ~20 lakh jobs; tourism >35 lakh a year.
  • Right to Work: MGNREGA 2005, 100 days, 625 districts → Viksit Bharat–G RAM G 2025.

Organised vs unorganised

  • Organised: regular, registered, Factories Act/Minimum Wages Act, PF, gratuity, paid leave, pension.
  • Unorganised: small, scattered, insecure, low-paid, no benefits.
  • 82 million organised vs 394 million unorganised (about 17% vs 83%).
  • 80% of rural households are small and marginal farmers.

Public vs private

  • Public = government owns assets (Railways, post office). Private = individuals/companies (TISCO, RIL).
  • Government spends where private sector will not: roads, bridges, harbours, power, irrigation.
  • Supports activities: electricity at affordable rates; fair prices and PDS.
  • Primary responsibility: health and education; IMR Odisha 36, MP 43.
19

Chapter Summary

The whole chapter in a few paragraphs

Economic activities are grouped into three sectors by their nature: the primary sector, which produces natural products by exploiting natural resources; the secondary sector, which manufactures natural products into other forms; and the tertiary sector, which supports production through services. The three are highly interdependent. To measure output we add the values of goods and services, counting only final goods and services, since intermediate goods are already included in their value. The sum gives GDP; India now also reports sector contributions as GVA, after adjusting for taxes and subsidies.

In developed countries the primary sector gave way to the secondary and then to the tertiary sector. In India the tertiary sector became the largest producer by 2017–18, but employment did not shift in the same way: industry’s output rose more than nine times while its employment rose about three times, and services’ output rose fourteen times against a five-fold rise in employment. More than half the workers therefore remain in agriculture, producing only about one-sixth of GVA — a situation of underemployment, or disguised unemployment, as in Laxmi’s family on two hectares.

More employment can be created by irrigation, transport and storage, cheap credit, industries in semi-rural areas, and expansion of education (about 20 lakh jobs) and tourism (over 35 lakh a year); in the short term the Right to Work — MGNREGA 2005, now the Viksit Bharat–G RAM G 2025 — guarantees 100 days of employment in rural areas.

Classified by employment conditions, the organised sector offers regular, registered, protected work while the unorganised sector — about 83 per cent of workers — offers low-paid, insecure work without benefits, and needs protection for landless labourers, small farmers, artisans, casual workers and street vendors. Classified by ownership, the public sector provides infrastructure, affordable electricity, fair prices and health and education that the private sector would not supply at a reasonable cost.
